did_you_know.text: Did you know? Psalm 48 is identified as a “song and psalm” and attributed to the sons of Korah, as stated in the psalm’s title.
Did you know? The psalm presents the greatness of the Lord specifically in connection with His city and holy mountain: “In the city of our God, His holy mountain.”
Did you know? Jerusalem is described with images of beauty, joy, and kingship: “beautiful in elevation,” “the joy of all the earth,” and “the city of the great King.”
Did you know? According to the psalm, God’s presence in the city’s palaces is what gives it its status as a fortress: “God is in her citadels; He is known as her stronghold.”
Did you know? The account of the kings’ confrontation with Jerusalem begins with their gathering together and passing before it: “The kings assembled; they passed by together.”
Did you know? The kings’ reaction to the sight of the city is described in three stages: they see it, are astonished, and then panic and hurry away.
Did you know? The kings’ fear is given the powerful image of an east wind capable of shattering the ships of Tarshish—a picture of storm and destructive force.
Did you know? The psalm emphasizes the correspondence between tradition and firsthand sight: “As we have heard, so we have seen,” in the city of the Lord of Hosts.

Did you know? Alongside the Lord’s greatness, the psalm also mentions His kindness, righteousness, and judgments; Jerusalem is therefore not merely an impressive city, but a place portrayed as filled with divine values.
Did you know? Near the end, there is a practical call to observe Zion: to walk around it and count its towers, so as to recognize its strength and remember it for generations.
